units.title: Where Does Human Dignity Come From?
units.sub: Two thousand years ago a letter home said, “throw it out if it’s a girl.” Why does reading it make us shudder today?

share.v: God created man in his own image. In God’s image he created him; male and female he created them.

blocks.h: In 1 BC a man named Hilarion wrote home from Alexandria to a woman named Alis. He asked her to look after the child, promised to send money as soon as he was paid, and said how could he ever forget her. At the end of the letter he calmly adds an instruction: if you give birth again, keep the baby if it is a boy, and throw it out if it is a girl.

What is most disturbing about this scrap of papyrus is that the writer does not seem cruel. He is just an ordinary husband who misses home. We shudder when we read it today, yet an ancient person could send greetings and write that line in the same breath. Where does our shudder come from?
God created man in his own image. In God’s image he created him; male and female he created them.
In the ancient world, people had price tags

Aristotle held that some people are slaves by nature and that being ruled is good for them, and he placed non-Greeks in this category. In Greece and Rome a father’s rights could include disposing of his own newborn child. How much a person was worth depended on bloodline, sex, status and usefulness.

An old ring is appraised at the pawnshop for three thousand dollars. The very same ring, once Grandma has left it to her granddaughter, is something she will not sell for any price. The weight of the gold has not changed. What changed is whose it is and who has loved it. The question of human worth works the same way: do you measure a person on the pawnshop scale, or do you ask whom that person belongs to?
One sentence from Genesis

In the ancient Near East, “image of God” was often a royal title: the king was God’s representative on earth. Many Old Testament scholars point out that Genesis 1 hands this title to every human being, male and female, whatever their status. This passage belongs to the Bible shared by Jews and Christians, and everyone today who looks down on another person has to face it.
Some saw it early, and some were slow to see it

In the fourth century, Gregory of Nyssa, commenting on Ecclesiastes 2:7, asked point-blank: if a human being is made in the image of God, who can set a price on him? If God Himself does not enslave those He created free, who dares to place his own power above God? This was extremely rare at the time. The Stoic Seneca also wrote in a letter that slaves should be treated kindly because they are people too, yet he still owned slaves himself and did not oppose slavery itself.

Gregory’s cry did not change his age. Augustine and many other church fathers accepted the hierarchy of their day, and the history of Christians owning slaves lasted more than a thousand years longer. The text had long been there. It took believers a very long time to take it seriously and live by it.
The table of 1948

On December 10, 1948, the United Nations General Assembly adopted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights in Paris, with 48 votes in favor, none against, and 8 abstentions. Article 1 says that all human beings are born free and equal in dignity and rights.

Seated at the drafting table were people of different convictions. Charles Malik of Lebanon was a Christian who often quoted Aquinas. The Chinese delegate Peng-chun Chang (P. C. Chang) was a student of John Dewey, deeply shaped by Confucianism, who often cited Mencius and insisted that the Declaration must not reflect only Western thought. It was Chang who proposed the word “conscience” in Article 1, and scholars see behind it the Confucian idea of ren (benevolence). The Declaration is not the exclusive achievement of Christianity; people from different civilizations contributed to it.
A family tree of the idea of equality

In recent years two books have stirred discussion. The political philosopher Larry Siedentop argues that the Western ideas of the individual and of equality can be traced from Paul all the way to the canon lawyers of the Middle Ages. The popular historian Tom Holland argues that even those who criticize Christianity often rely on moral intuitions that Christianity shaped. Holland describes himself as a cultural Christian. He is writing the history of the West, and does not claim that these ideas belong to Christianity alone.

items.h: Western equality and individual dignity were nurtured mainly by Paul, the church fathers and medieval canon law. Secular human-rights language inherited this legacy and forgot where it came from.
Stoic philosophy, Jewish tradition, Roman law and Confucianism, among others, all supplied resources. Christianity is one important stream among them, not the only source.

Critics such as Kenan Malik point out that the church long defended hierarchy and also divided people by their faith. Equality that includes everyone truly emerged only after the idea of a divinely ordained order loosened.

blocks.h: The argument is not over. One thing, though, is certain: many of today’s most forceful defenders of human rights are people who do not believe in God, and they too live out a human conscience. The Bible’s explanation covers this as well: every person bears the image of God, whether or not he believes.
Below we separate historical fact, interpretation and inference.
Oxyrhynchus Papyrus 744, from 1 BC, does record a husband’s instruction to abandon a baby girl. The letter proves that this happened, but it cannot by itself tell us how common abandoning babies was.
The emperor Valentinian formally legislated against infanticide in AD 374. In earlier Greek and Roman law and custom, a father held the power of life and death over his children.

The Universal Declaration of Human Rights was adopted in 1948 with 48 votes in favor and 8 abstentions. Peng-chun Chang and Charles Malik were both central drafters, and the word “conscience” was proposed by Chang.

“Image of God” comes from the ancient Near Eastern way of addressing a king, and Genesis extends it to all of humanity. This is a very influential interpretation among Old Testament scholars, though the details are still debated.
How much Christianity contributed to Western ideas of equality and human rights is still debated by historians. Siedentop, Holland and their critics do not agree.

If human dignity is inborn and does not depend on ability or usefulness, it needs a foundation more solid than social consensus. God’s making people in His own image is one powerful account of that foundation. Atheists can also defend human rights firmly. This inference asks about the foundation, and does not say they lack morality.
He put a price on you

The Bible says human dignity is given by God, so no one can take it away, and not even sin wipes it out. When James rebukes the tongue, he reminds us that even the person being cursed carries this honor.
With it we bless our God and Father, and with it we curse men who are made in the image of God.

The highest proof of this dignity is on the cross. In the ancient world the cheapest person was the slave, and the Son of God chose to go to that very place and die for those who were still His enemies.

who, existing in the form of God, didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men. And being found in human form, he humbled himself, becoming obedient to the point of death, yes, the death of the cross.

The righteous God will not allow anyone to be priced, and the good God Himself paid the highest price. Whatever the pawnshop scale says you are worth does not count. He loved you while you were still a sinner.
But God commends his own love toward us, in that while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.

Today, at a convenience store, on the MRT or at a construction site, pick someone you would normally not look at twice: a clerk, a cleaning aunty, a foreign caregiver. Say quietly in your heart: this person was made in the image of God, and Christ died for him too.
Meditate: is there a pawnshop scale in my heart? Whom have I weighed by education, income, looks or nationality? And what do I use to weigh myself?

Prayer: Father who created me, thank You for making me in Your image, and for showing on the cross how precious I am to You. Forgive me for looking down on those You have made, and forgive me for looking down on myself. Give me eyes to recognize Your image in every face. In the name of Jesus, amen.
321 Life Application

items: Jesus is my example: He was in the form of God, yet took the form of a servant. I too will set aside my status and serve someone who is of no use to me.
People matter more than tasks: coworkers, migrant workers and the elders at home are not tools for getting things done. See the person first, and then talk about the task.
Change your mindset: when you move from the human viewpoint (what are you worth?) to God’s viewpoint (whom do you belong to?), you no longer need comparison to prove yourself.

blocks.h: This week: learn the name of someone you see often but whose name you do not know. Ask for it, write it down, and greet that person by name next time.
Pass it on: why do you think people have dignity? If a person is of no use to society, does he still have worth? Where does that worth come from?
Quiz

quiz.q: Who proposed the word “conscience” in Article 1 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights?
o: Peng-chun Chang
Eleanor Roosevelt
Charles Malik
quiz.e: Chang proposed “conscience,” and scholars see behind it the Confucian idea of ren (benevolence). The Declaration is the shared achievement of many civilizations.

quiz.q: How do many Old Testament scholars explain “the image of God” in Genesis?
o: It only means that people look like God in appearance
It applies only to believers
It extends the honorific of ancient kings to everyone
quiz.e: In the ancient Near East a king was often called the image of God, but Genesis says every person is.

quiz.q: Looking at it honestly, what is the history of the church and human dignity?
o: The church has always stood on the right side
Some saw it early, and many believers long failed to live by it
The Bible has nothing to do with this issue
quiz.e: Gregory of Nyssa questioned slavery very early, but the church as a whole took an extremely long time to arrive at that point.

units.title: Hospitals: Mercy Becomes an Institution
units.sub: One act of kindness can save one person. A hospital that opens its doors every day can catch every stranger who cannot pay.

share.v: “The King will answer them, ‘Most certainly I tell you, because you did it to one of the least of these my brothers, you did it to me.’

blocks.h: In fourth-century Asia Minor, a church leader raised a complex of buildings outside the city, with lodgings for the poor, guest houses for travelers and a place to treat the sick. His friend compared it to the wonders of the world. What made people marvel wasn’t how grand the buildings were. It was the people living inside: a crowd of poor folk who were of no use to anyone.
“The King will answer them, ‘Most certainly I tell you, because you did it to one of the least of these my brothers, you did it to me.’
Basil of Caesarea

Before Basil (about 330–379) became a bishop, his region was struck by famine after a drought, and he personally organized soup kitchens and handed out food to the poor. In 370 he became bishop of Caesarea, and outside the city he built this complex that later generations called the “Basiliad”; the emperor Valens even donated land. Today it is generally regarded as one of the earliest Christian hospitals established for the poor.

Donating one bag of blood can save one person. A blood bank is different: a stranger brought in from a car accident in the middle of the night can get blood right away, with no need for a kind person to happen to walk by. A hospital does the same thing. It stores up act after act of mercy and turns them into a place anyone in need can find.
An honest look: other civilizations had them too

Christians did not invent places of healing. The Greek temples of Asclepius had case records as early as the fourth century BC. From about 100 BC Rome had medical facilities treating slaves, gladiators and soldiers. Buddhist traditions in India and Sri Lanka also have records of caring for the sick, though the dates and nature of those sources still need sorting out. The Islamic world later built an outstanding hospital system.
Islamic hospitals

Damascus had a hospital by 706/707. The earliest general hospital is generally attributed to Baghdad in 805 under Harun al-Rashid, and by the tenth century Baghdad had five more. Most of these hospitals were open to everyone, and the law forbade turning away patients who could not pay. This history deserves the respect of Christians.
Reaching the Chinese world

Peter Parker was the first full-time Protestant medical missionary to China. In 1835 he opened an eye clinic in Canton (Guangzhou), and in its first year it treated more than 2,000 patients. He also preached to patients and trained Chinese students. The clinic closed in 1840 because of the conflict between China and Britain, reopened in 1842 and later became Canton’s Pok Tsai Hospital. In Taiwan, James Maxwell of the English Presbyterian Church began work in 1865, and the work of Maxwell and his son later left behind Sin-Lau Hospital in Tainan.
Nightingale and the plague argument

At sixteen, Nightingale experienced what she described as a call from God. In 1854 she led nurses to Scutari, in 1860 she opened a nursing school, and she was also the first woman member of Britain’s Royal Statistical Society. Her faith did not fit traditional orthodoxy: she believed all people would finally be saved, often criticized the church, and even held that care in secular hospitals was usually better than in religious ones. Using her as a simple poster for Christian apologetics would be unfair to her.

The sociologist Rodney Stark argued that in the two great plagues of 165 and 251, Christians stayed in the cities to care for the sick, and so fewer of them died and their faith became more attractive. This is an influential inference, not a settled conclusion.

items.h: Basic care (water, food) really can lower death rates. Christian networks of mutual aid helped survival and growth, and they also let people see how faith faces suffering.
Ancient death rates and numbers of believers are both hard to estimate precisely, church writings may also flatter themselves, and growth can’t be credited to plagues alone.

blocks.h: Below we separate historical fact, interpretation and inference from faith.
In the later fourth century, outside Caesarea, Basil built a complex including lodgings for the poor, guest houses and a hospital.
The Islamic world built a hospital system in the eighth to tenth centuries that was widely open to people; Greece, Rome and South Asia each also had earlier places of healing.
Peter Parker opened an eye clinic in Canton in 1835, and James Maxwell later began medical mission work in Taiwan.
Christian institutions made an important contribution to the formation of “hospitals for the poor”; whether they count as “the earliest” depends on how a hospital is defined.
Care during plagues caused fewer Christian deaths and drove the growth of the church. This is Stark’s thesis, and it can’t yet count as settled.

Jesus linked the sick with Himself, and these words gave mercy a lasting motive and made caring for “useless” people part of worship. This is a reading from faith, and medical workers who don’t believe serve people with mercy too.
He saw, and He was moved with compassion
The story of hospitals begins with a Healer who walked through towns and villages.

Jesus went about all the cities and the villages, teaching in their synagogues and preaching the Good News of the Kingdom, and healing every disease and every sickness among the people. But when he saw the multitudes, he was moved with compassion for them because they were harassed and scattered, like sheep without a shepherd.

His mercy went all the way to the cross. The Bible doesn’t promise that every illness will be healed, and being sick doesn’t mean a lack of faith or a punishment. What the Bible says is this: the Lord who bore those wounds is with those who suffer, and He paid the price for our sins.
But he was pierced for our transgressions. He was crushed for our iniquities. The punishment that brought our peace was on him; and by his wounds we are healed.

The righteous God cares about those who cannot pay, and the good God Himself carries human pain. The risen Lord will in the end wipe away all sickness and pain, and today we are simply doing, a little ahead of time, some of what He is going to do.
Think of someone lying in a hospital bed right now, or a nurse or caregiver working the night shift. Write down that person’s name and pray for one minute.
Meditate: is my mercy a passing feeling, or has it already become a settled habit? Who is waiting for me to come and see them one more time?

Prayer: Lord of mercy, You saw the harassed and scattered, and You were moved with compassion. Please comfort those in sickness and pain today, and strengthen those who care for them. Make my mercy more than a passing feeling, and turn it into lasting love. In the name of Jesus, amen.
321 Life Application

items: Jesus is my example: He walked through towns and villages and was moved with compassion when He saw people. I too will slow my steps and see the sick and the caregivers around me.
People matter more than tasks: when visiting the sick, don’t rush to give answers or rush to explain why they got sick. Staying with them is love.
Build God’s kingdom system: Basil turned mercy into an institution. A small group can set up a regular care rota so that no one gets forgotten.

blocks.h: This week: visit someone who is sick or a long-term caregiver, or share one concrete load, such as giving a ride, buying groceries or watching the children. If you yourself have an ongoing physical problem, please see a doctor; this unit isn’t medical advice.
Pass it on: when you or your family were sick, whose care do you remember most? Why do you think a person would be willing to care for a total stranger?
Quiz

quiz.q: Who was the complex Basil built outside Caesarea mainly for?
o: Soldiers of the Roman legions
The poor, travelers and the sick
Officials of the imperial court
quiz.e: This complex took in the poor, received travelers and treated the sick, and it is regarded as one of the early Christian hospitals established for the poor.

quiz.q: Which statement about the history of hospitals is fairest?
o: Only Christianity had hospitals
The Islamic world had no hospitals
Several civilizations had medical institutions, and Christianity was one important contributor
quiz.e: Greece, Rome, South Asia and the Islamic world all made their own contributions, and the hospitals of Baghdad were especially outstanding.

quiz.q: Where did Peter Parker open his eye clinic in 1835?
o: Canton (Guangzhou)
Tainan
Shanghai
quiz.e: His eye clinic opened in Canton and later developed into Pok Tsai Hospital.

units.title: The University: A Community in Pursuit of Truth
units.sub: One death, three hanged roommates and a crowd of students who left overnight: that’s how the university actually began.

share.v: The fear of Yahweh is the beginning of knowledge; but the foolish despise wisdom and instruction.

blocks.h: In Oxford in the early thirteenth century, a student accidentally killed a woman and fled overnight. The townspeople couldn’t catch him, so they seized his three roommates. A few days later, on the orders of the English king, three young men who knew nothing about the matter were hanged outside the town.

The teachers and students responded by leaving together. The chronicle says about three thousand went (the number may not be precise). Some went to Reading, and some went to a little town on the edge of the marshes called Cambridge. A famous university began with a group of students running from the gallows.
The fear of Yahweh is the beginning of knowledge; but the foolish despise wisdom and instruction.
The university started as a guild

The Latin word universitas originally had nothing to do with the “universe.” It referred to a guild: a corporate body of teachers and students. Students from out of town in Bologna formed mutual-aid societies, because local law could hold a foreign student liable for debts owed by someone from his home region. Together they hired teachers, and together they negotiated terms with the city.

Imagine a group of overseas Chinese students studying in Taipei who discover that a landlord can seize your luggage because someone from your hometown owes rent. So everyone forms an overseas students’ association, goes to negotiate with the landlord together, and while they’re at it, jointly hires a good teacher to run a class. The medieval university is what that kind of mutual-aid society looks like once it has grown up: it learned solidarity first and only slowly became a temple of learning.
The church as promoter and as manager

In 1179 Pope Alexander III ruled that church schools could not charge a fee for granting a license to teach and must give the license to those who qualified. In 1229 the teachers and students of Paris went on strike over an injustice in the courts, and in 1231 Pope Gregory IX issued the bull Parens scientiarum (“Mother of the Sciences”), allowing the university to set its own statutes and to suspend lectures in cases of judicial injustice. In that era, an academic body that could say “no” to kings and bishops was something very new.
“Love God with your whole mind”

Theology was one of the three higher faculties of the medieval university. The historian Edward Grant argues that the university was the institutional tool Western Europe used to organize and absorb new knowledge. These scholars read Aristotle and also argued with him: believing in a rational Creator made them feel that studying the created world was a worthwhile thing to do.
Thirteen Christian universities in the Chinese world

From the end of the nineteenth century on, mission societies founded a number of universities in China, and the archives of Yale Divinity School list 13. They include St. John’s in Shanghai (founded 1879), Soochow (1900), Cheeloo (whose predecessors include the Tengchow College run by Calvin Mateer from 1882), Nanking (1910), Ginling Women’s College (planned from 1913, opened 1915) and Yenching (1919, with John Leighton Stuart as president).

Yenching’s motto was “Freedom through Truth for Service.” Ginling’s first graduating class in 1919 were the first women in China to earn officially recognized Bachelor of Arts degrees, and its president, Wu Yi-fang, was the first Chinese woman to head a university. During the Nanjing Massacre of 1937, Minnie Vautrin, who was acting head of the college, turned the campus into a shelter for nearly ten thousand people.

In 1952, during China’s reorganization of university departments, all of these universities were dissolved and merged into other schools. Today’s Peking University campus is the old Yenching site. Soochow’s alumni re-established their school in Taiwan.
Harvard’s first rule

In 1636 the Massachusetts colonial legislature voted to establish a college. The 1643 pamphlet New England’s First Fruits spells out the motive: a dread of leaving the churches an illiterate ministry once their pastors had gone to their rest. The student rules required them to understand that the main end of life and study was to know God and Jesus Christ, citing John 17:3.

Half of the early graduates became ministers, but by the 1760s only about 15% did. Harvard also ran an Indian College, with very few students and only one graduate. Its motto once read “Truth for Christ and the Church”; the one in common use today is “Truth” (Veritas). This change can be read in different ways, but it did happen.
Don’t rush to say the university is uniquely Christian

As early as 859, a Muslim woman named Fatima al-Fihri founded the Qarawiyyin mosque in Fez, Morocco, which later developed into a place of higher learning. The Nizamiyya college was established in Baghdad in 1065, and al-Ghazali taught there from 1091. The scholar George Makdisi argues that European universities borrowed some features from Islamic colleges. Other scholars consider the two institutions fundamentally different, since the university was a corporate body with legal self-government while the Islamic college relied on charitable endowment. This debate is still going on.

items.h: Walter Rüegg and others argue that the university, with its self-governing corporate status and universally recognized degrees, was a creation of medieval Europe, and that until shown otherwise it should be regarded as the sole source of later university models.

Makdisi and others point out that institutions such as degrees and chairs may have been influenced by Islamic colleges. Critics caution that similarity doesn’t necessarily mean descent, and the route of transmission remains to be proven.

Different civilizations each developed their own forms of higher education, and China’s academies (shuyuan) and Imperial Academy (taixue) also have a long tradition. Treating any one form as “the real university” involves a choice of definition.

blocks.h: The church has also shut the door

In 1277 Bishop Tempier of Paris condemned 219 propositions, aimed at scholars in the faculty of arts. The historian of physics Pierre Duhem once argued that this condemnation actually set scientific thought free, but today no specialist agrees that modern science began in 1277. In 1633 Galileo was convicted of being vehemently suspected of heresy and sentenced to house arrest for life, and his book was banned. Historians remind us that the case also involved academic and court politics, but the verdict was the church’s; in 1992 Pope John Paul II acknowledged that the theologians of that time had been wrong.
Let’s separate fact, interpretation and inference.
The origins of the University of Cambridge are usually traced to the scholars who left Oxford in 1209; Pope John XXII formally recognized it as a place of higher learning in 1318.
The details of the Oxford incident (three men hanged, three thousand leaving) come mainly from medieval chronicles. The general picture is credible, but the numbers should be held loosely.

Bologna’s use of 1088 as its founding year was set by a nineteenth-century committee led by Carducci; some historians think it didn’t qualify as a “university” until after the 1150s. Don’t treat 1088 as an exact founding record.
In 1952, China’s Christian universities were dissolved in the reorganization of departments and merged into other schools.
The relationship between medieval European universities and Islamic colleges is still debated among historians.

Believing that the world comes from a rational Creator was one of the forces that moved people to study the world. This is a reading from faith, and history itself doesn’t draw that conclusion; many scholars who don’t believe in God are just as loyal to the truth, and that also deserves respect.
Truth is a Person, and worth loving with your mind

The Bible places the starting point of wisdom in the fear of God. People who fear God know they are not the center of the world, so they are willing to be taught and willing to be corrected by the facts. In history, the church has looked least like the church exactly when it treated itself as the truth.
in whom all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden.

Christians believe that truth, in the end, is more than a set of propositions. Jesus said, “I am the way, the truth, and the life.” This Truth did not protect Himself with statutes and courts. He stood on trial before Pilate and was nailed to a cross. God’s wisdom is displayed in the place that looks least like wisdom.
Because the foolishness of God is wiser than men, and the weakness of God is stronger than men.

God is faithful. The world He made can stand up to investigation, and His word can stand up to hard questions. So people who pursue truth don’t need to be afraid of questions, and they don’t need to use questions to prove they’re smarter than everyone else.
Now concerning things sacrificed to idols: We know that we all have knowledge. Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up.
Find the school you attended or your child’s school, and look up its motto and founding story. Think about this: what did these people build this school for in the first place?
Meditate: Do I study and work in order to know what is true and to serve people, or in order to beat people? When was the last time the facts changed my mind?

Prayer: God who gives wisdom, You are the source of all truth. Forgive me for using knowledge as a weapon, and forgive the church for having been afraid of truth. Lord Jesus, You are the truth. Make me love You with all my heart, all my soul and all my mind, and use my mind to serve people. In Jesus’ name, amen.
321 Life Application

items: The Bible is my standard: the fear of God is the beginning of knowledge, not the end of it. Faith gives you the courage to ask questions and a heart willing to be taught.
Humility overcomes pride: a degree is grace, not rank. The self-centered use knowledge to step on people; the selfless use knowledge to lift people up.
People matter more than tasks: the last word of Yenching’s motto is service. Ask yourself: whom is the thing you’ve learned serving right now?

blocks.h: This week: find a student or a younger colleague and ask, “What have you been learning lately?” Listen carefully for ten minutes without giving advice. Then pick a good book you wouldn’t normally read, and read one chapter.
Pass it on: Do you know how universities first came about? Why do you think a person should pursue truth, and not only useful knowledge?
Quiz

quiz.q: What did the Latin word universitas originally mean?
o: The universe
A guild of teachers and students
A church school
quiz.e: It originally referred to a body of teachers and students, a kind of guild, and had nothing to do with the universe.

quiz.q: How should we regard the University of Bologna’s date of 1088?
o: It was set retrospectively by a committee in the nineteenth century, and some historians think the university came much later
A founding certificate from 1088 survives
The pope personally approved it in 1088
quiz.e: The imperial charter of 1158 is the earlier document; 1088 is a later retrospective date.

quiz.q: On the church and the university, what is this unit’s honest conclusion?
o: The church never interfered with scholarship
The church only suppressed scholarship
The church was an important promoter, and it also suppressed scholarship at times
quiz.e: A papal bull protected the university’s self-government; the condemnation of 1277 and the Galileo case are the other side.

units.title: Abolition: The Conscience of a Generation
units.sub: Christians led the abolition of the slave trade. Christians also opened the Bible to defend it. Both things must be said.

share.v: There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither slave nor free man, there is neither male nor female; for you are all one in Christ Jesus.

blocks.h: In 1688, in Germantown, Pennsylvania, four Quakers wrote out a sheet of paper and put a question to their fellow believers: how can we buy and sell human beings? It is one of the earliest antislavery documents in North America. The meeting that received it passed it along from one body to another, and in the end set it aside.

After that sheet of paper, it would be more than a hundred years before Britain abolished the slave trade. Treating human beings as goods was once regarded as perfectly ordinary business, and many devout people took part in it.
He has shown you, O man, what is good. What does the LORD require of you, but to act justly, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with your God?
The ugliest part first

Over several centuries the transatlantic slave trade carried off about 12.5 million Africans, and many died on the way. The participants included Christian nations, merchants and ship captains. In the American South, pastors and theologians published large numbers of works citing Ephesians and 1 Timothy to argue that slavery is biblical. The founding of the Southern Baptist Convention in 1845 was linked to the dispute over slavery, and in 1995 the Convention publicly repented of it.
Servants, be obedient to those who according to the flesh are your masters, with fear and trembling, in singleness of your heart, as to Christ,
Passages like these were among the most quoted of the day. Any Christian who talks honestly about abolition must face this first: the Bible has been used to bind people.
A conscience awakened step by step

items: 1688, the Germantown protest: the question put by four Quakers, which was set aside at the time.

John Woolman (1720–1772): a Quaker tailor who visited slaveholders one household at a time and pleaded with them earnestly. He refused to wear clothing colored with dyes produced by slave labor and to buy other slave-produced goods, and in 1754 published Some Considerations on the Keeping of Negroes.
Anthony Benezet (1713–1784): a Philadelphia teacher who opened a school for Black children and gathered facts for his writings, which influenced British abolitionists who came later.
Thomas Clarkson (1760–1846): after writing a prize-winning essay at Cambridge in 1785, he gave his whole life to investigation, traveling from port to port gathering evidence.

William Wilberforce (1759–1833): a British Member of Parliament who came to faith and brought motion after motion beginning in 1789. The bill abolishing the slave trade passed in 1807, and a few days before his death in 1833, the bill abolishing slavery made decisive progress.

John Newton (1725–1807): author of “Amazing Grace.” He had been the captain of a slave ship and kept sailing for several years after he came to faith. Only many years later did he repent publicly, and in 1788 he published a testimony in support of abolition.

blocks.h: Changing a conscience is like chipping at a great rock. You strike once and nothing happens. You strike a thousand times and it still looks the same. The rock finally splits on one particular blow, and not because that blow was any stronger, but because everyone before had never put down the hammer.
The enslaved were not supporting actors

History classes often tell abolition as an act of kindness by white people, and that is incomplete. Olaudah Equiano published his autobiography in 1789; it became a bestseller of the day and he toured giving talks. He was a Christian, though scholars still discuss where he was born. The slave uprising in Haiti began in 1791 under leaders such as Toussaint Louverture, and an independent nation was founded in 1804. The “Baptist War” in Jamaica in 1831–32 was led by the Baptist deacon Samuel Sharpe and hastened Britain’s decision.
The law also had a bitter side. In 1833 Britain paid £20 million in compensation, and it went to the slaveholders. Those who were freed received nothing.
How historians explain it

In 1944 Eric Williams argued that abolition came mainly from the decline of the Caribbean sugar economy. In 1977 Seymour Drescher rebutted him, arguing that the sugar economy was not in decline at the time and that abolition actually hurt British interests. Most historians today would say that religious mobilization, economic change, resistance by the enslaved and Enlightenment ideas all played a part, and that how much weight each deserves is still debated.
Today

An estimate published in 2022 by the International Labour Organization and others: in 2021 about 50 million people worldwide were living in modern slavery, about 28 million of them in forced labor and about 22 million in forced marriage.
Separating fact from interpretation.
The Germantown protest of 1688, Britain’s Slave Trade Act of 1807 and its Slavery Abolition Act of 1833 are all established historical facts.
Christians widely cited the Bible to defend slavery, and many Christians took part in the slave trade.
The faith of evangelicals and Quakers was one of the main driving forces of the British abolition movement. Most historians agree on this, though how much weight it deserves is still debated.
The resistance of the enslaved had a great influence on the course of abolition, for example the Haitian Revolution and the Jamaican uprising; the exact degree of influence is still under discussion.
The number of people in modern slavery is a model-based estimate. The actual number is hard to pin down precisely.

“Made in the image of God” and “you are all one in Christ” give the deepest grounds for opposing slavery. This is theological inference. It cannot cancel out the failures of the church, and it does not mean that only Christians can oppose slavery.
A dialogue of viewpoints
Why didn’t the New Testament directly tell people to abolish slavery?

items.h: The New Testament teaches slaves to obey and does not condemn the institution itself. Passages such as 1 Timothy 6:1 gave slaveholders confidence. Abolition later came from human moral progress, and the Bible was actually an obstacle.

The New Testament was written to a minority with no political power, and a direct attack on the system could not have succeeded. It planted seeds beneath the system: slaves and masters have one Master (Ephesians 6:9), and Philemon asks the master to receive Onesimus as a beloved brother. 1 Timothy 1:10 condemns those who steal people. But that the seeds sprouted so slowly is also something the church must admit with shame.

blocks.h: He hears the groans of the captives

When the God of the Bible first introduces Himself, He is the God who led slaves out of Egypt. The law contains a provision that was unusual in the ancient world: a slave who has escaped must not be handed back to his master.

You shall not deliver to his master a servant who has escaped from his master to you. He shall dwell with you, among you, in the place which he shall choose within one of your gates, where it pleases him best. You shall not oppress him.

When Paul sent the runaway slave Onesimus back, he wrote a very short letter asking the master to receive him as more than a slave, as a beloved brother. The letter does not announce the abolition of the system, but it shakes the system from the inside. How long can you go on buying and selling someone you call brother?

For perhaps he was therefore separated from you for a while that you would have him forever, no longer as a slave, but more than a slave, a beloved brother—especially to me, but how much rather to you, both in the flesh and in the Lord.

The deepest reason lies on the cross. Christ took the form of a servant. He was sold in our place, whipped and nailed to a cross, and rose on the third day. With His own blood He paid the price of redemption. The slave market put a price on people. The cross shows the worth of every human being in God’s eyes: His only Son.
Stand firm therefore in the liberty by which Christ has made us free, and don’t be entangled again with a yoke of bondage.
Look at the clothes you are wearing today and the phone in your hand. On the supply chains of these things are people you do not know. Be quiet for a moment and pray for them for one minute.

Meditate: what is one thing society treats as normal today that Christians a hundred years from now will ask me about: how could you have done that? What Scriptures have I used to find excuses for my own convenience?

Prayer: Lord who sets the captives free, You heard the groans from beneath the ship’s deck, and You hear the groans today in factories and back alleys. We repent that the church once used Your word to bind people. Thank You, Lord Jesus, for taking the form of a servant and redeeming us with Your precious blood. Give us the conscience of Woolman and the endurance of Clarkson. In the name of Jesus, amen.
321 Life Application

items: The Bible is my standard: a standard is not something to find support for our own interests. When you read Scripture, ask: what kind of heart does this passage finally lead people toward in Christ?

Humility overcomes pride: we may give thanks for Christian abolitionists, but we must not treat their achievement as our own glory. Only by admitting the church’s failures do we have the right to speak of the gospel.
People matter more than tasks: employees, migrant workers, caregivers and delivery riders are not tools. My relationship with them is the real state of my faith.

blocks.h: This week: look up the supply-chain information for a brand you often buy, or find out about the anti-trafficking organizations in your area and see what you could give to or serve with. If you or someone you know is being controlled, has had documents confiscated or is being forced to work, please contact the local police or labor and immigration services.
Pass it on: what do you find most disappointing in history: that people did evil, or that good people thought it was normal?
Quiz

quiz.q: Which statement about Christians and slavery is most honest?
o: Christians opposed slavery from the very beginning
Christians were an important force in abolition, and many also used the Bible to defend slavery
Christians had nothing to do with slavery
quiz.e: Both are true. This unit tells both.

quiz.q: When Britain abolished slavery in 1833, who received the £20 million in compensation?
o: The slaveholders
The freed slaves
The church
quiz.e: The freed people received nothing, and that is the painful part of this history.

quiz.q: What does the Haitian Revolution, which began in 1791, remind us of?
o: Abolition depended entirely on the British Parliament
Africans never resisted
The enslaved themselves were among the leading actors in the fight for freedom
quiz.e: Haiti became independent in 1804. The struggle of Black people themselves was no supporting role.

units.title: Women: The Ones Who Were Seen
units.sub: The disciples were astonished to see Jesus talking with a woman. That astonishment is where this story begins.

share.v: God created man in his own image. In God’s image he created him; male and female he created them.

blocks.h: In 1 BC a husband working in Egypt wrote to his pregnant wife. Besides sending greetings, he added in passing: if it is a boy, keep it; if it is a girl, throw it out. The letter survives today on papyrus, and its tone is as ordinary as an instruction to buy groceries.
About thirty years later, at a well in Judea, a rabbi asked a Samaritan woman for a drink of water. When the disciples came back, they were stunned.
Just then, his disciples came. They marveled that he was speaking with a woman; yet no one said, “What are you looking for?” or, “Why do you speak with her?”
That world

Oxyrhynchus Papyrus 744 proves that the abandonment of baby girls happened, but it cannot by itself tell us how common it was. The situation of women in the Greco-Roman world varied greatly by region and class. There were wealthy female patrons and there were female slaves with no rights at all, so it is not wise to paint everything with one brush.
In the Jewish setting, Josephus, restating the law in Antiquities 4.219, says that women are not to serve as witnesses.
What Jesus did

items: Conversation: at the well He spoke with the Samaritan woman about worship and the Messiah. In John’s Gospel, the first time He plainly says that He is the Messiah is to this woman (John 4:26).

Companionship: Luke records a group of women who followed Him through town after town, and their names are preserved: Mary Magdalene, Joanna and Susanna. Part of the expenses of the disciples came from them (Luke 8:1-3).
Teaching: Mary sat at His feet and listened to His teaching, which was the posture of a disciple. He said she had chosen the good part (Luke 10:38-42).
Seeing: the woman bent over for eighteen years and the woman who had bled for twelve years: He stopped for both, and called them a “daughter of Abraham” and “Daughter” (Luke 13:12-16; Mark 5:34).

blocks.h: An important meeting has just ended, and the first person the boss phones to share the news is the part-time student worker whom nobody in the whole company wanted to listen to. The morning of the resurrection has that flavor.
The first witnesses of the resurrection

All four Gospels place women at the empty tomb. In an environment that did not readily accept women’s testimony, this is hardly a clever arrangement for anyone inventing a story. For this reason scholars such as Richard Bauckham conclude that real memory has been preserved here. The disciples’ reaction is honest too: they took it for nonsense.
After the gospel spread

In Romans 16 Paul greets a number of women coworkers: Phoebe, a deacon of the church at Cenchreae; Priscilla; Junia. Rodney Stark argues that the early church held a special attraction for women because it opposed the abandonment of infants and discouraged child marriage. This is an influential sociological argument but not a settled one, and some historians criticize his data.

It was even more so in the modern missionary movement. From the late nineteenth century on, in many mission societies female missionaries outnumbered male ones. Lottie Moon (1840–1912) of the Southern Baptists went to Shandong in 1873, later gave her own money and food to people in famine, and died in 1912 on the voyage home. The Christmas offering named after her continues to this day.
Foot binding and girls’ schools

Around 1874, missionaries and believers in Xiamen had already started anti-foot-binding societies. In 1895 the Englishwoman Alicia Little founded the Natural Foot Society in Shanghai; she herself was not a missionary. Chinese reformers such as Kang Youwei and Liang Qichao also pushed hard for it. The credit cannot all go to the church, but the church was indeed one of the early drivers.
In Taiwan, George Mackay opened the Tamsui Girls’ School in 1884. His wife, Chang Tsung-ming, a local Taiwanese woman who married him in 1878, later also took part in the work of the school.
The other side that must also be told

The church father Tertullian once called women “the devil’s gateway.” Aquinas, following Aristotle, called the individual woman a “defective and misbegotten male,” while also holding that woman belongs to God’s intention for human nature. In early modern Europe the witch hunts killed an estimated forty to sixty thousand people, most of them women, and Catholics and Protestants alike took part. To this day there are women in churches who are abused and then told to be patient. These are shameful, not exceptions.
The history of faith is most easily told with only the good side.
The Gospels record women following Jesus, funding His ministry and being the first to witness the empty tomb. This is a fact of the text.
George Mackay opened the Tamsui Girls’ School in 1884.

That women were the earliest witnesses of the resurrection makes it more likely that this account preserves real memory. Most scholars take this argument seriously, though some propose other explanations.
Christians were one of the driving forces of the foot-binding reform, and native Chinese reformers were just as crucial.
The early church had a higher proportion of women and gave them better standing. Stark’s argument is influential, but the evidence is still debated.

“Male and female He created them in His image” and the way Jesus treated women are the basis on which Christians affirm women’s dignity. This is theological inference, and the church’s history of putting it into practice has not been consistent.
A dialogue of viewpoints

Can women serve as pastors and elders? Within evangelicalism there are two main positions. Both uphold the Bible and share the same core faith. This unit sets them side by side and does not rule between them.

items.h: Men and women are equally honored, but God gives them different roles. The teaching and governing office of elder in the church is held by qualified men. 1 Timothy 2:11-14 appeals to the order of creation, and not only to the convenience of the culture of the day. Both men and women are called, and the range of service remains wide.

Gifts are not divided by sex, and offices should not be either. Phoebe, Junia, Priscilla and the women prophets show that women actually took part. 1 Timothy 2:12 is an instruction for the particular situation in Ephesus, and should be read together with Galatians 3:28 and Acts 2:17-18.

blocks.h: He sees

Right at the beginning, Genesis places male and female together in “the image of God.” In the ancient world “the image of God” was mostly a royal title, but the Bible gives it to every person, and to every woman.
God created man in his own image. In God’s image he created him; male and female he created them.

On the morning of the resurrection, the first name Jesus called was “Mary.” At one word she recognized Him. Then He sent her to tell the disciples. In the resurrection appearances recorded by John, the person in the first conversation is this woman who had once been possessed by seven demons.

Jesus said to her, “Mary.” She turned and said to him, “Rabboni!” which is to say, “Teacher!” Jesus said to her, “Don’t hold me, for I haven’t yet ascended to my Father; but go to my brothers and tell them, ‘I am ascending to my Father and your Father, to my God and your God.’” Mary Magdalene came and told the disciples that she had seen the Lord, and that he had said these things to her.
Paul saw the same thing in Christ: the cross and the resurrection changed the foundation on which people treat one another.
There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither slave nor free man, there is neither male nor female; for you are all one in Christ Jesus.
Think of a woman who helped you along your path of faith: Mom, Grandma, a Sunday school teacher or a sister in the church. Write her one sentence of thanks today, and thank God for her.
Meditate: do my words and habits make the women around me feel unseen? If I am a woman, do I believe that the Lord has called my name?

Prayer: Lord who sees me, You waited at a well for a woman everyone avoided, and at the tomb You called Mary by name. Thank You for dying and rising again for us. We repent for the times the church has hurt women. Heal the sisters who are wounded, protect those who are victims, and teach us to honor one another. In the name of Jesus, amen.
321 Life Application

items: Jesus is my example: He was willing to stop at a well and listen to someone others avoided. I too will go and see those who are overlooked.
People matter more than tasks: whether your church is complementarian or egalitarian, let every sister be respected and heard.

920: every relationship is my 2, lived out selflessly. Husband and wife do not contend over who is greater, and they practice mutual submission. The Bible never tells anyone to use “submission” to cover up violence; if you are suffering domestic violence, please put safety and professional help first.

blocks.h: This week: write a card or send a message thanking a sister specifically for her service. If you know someone suffering domestic violence, help her contact the local protection hotline or a social worker (in Taiwan, dial 113).
Pass it on: when and why do you think a society’s view of women began to change?
Quiz

quiz.q: What did the disciples find astonishing when they saw Jesus at the well?
o: Casting out demons
Talking with a woman
Drinking wine
quiz.e: John 4:27. In that setting, this was very unusual.

quiz.q: What is this unit’s position on women holding church office?
o: It sets the complementarian and egalitarian views side by side and does not rule between them
Only the egalitarian view is biblical
Only the complementarian view is biblical
quiz.e: This is a peripheral debate. Both sides uphold the Bible and share the same core faith.

quiz.q: Which statement about the foot-binding reform is most accurate?
o: It was entirely the missionaries’ achievement
No Christians took part in it
Christians were one of the drivers, and Chinese reformers were also crucial
quiz.e: Alicia Little, the anti-foot-binding society in Xiamen, and Kang Youwei and Liang Qichao all had a part.

units.title: Orphans and Children
units.sub: A world once let fathers decide whether a baby lived or died, and a rabbi took the children into His arms. This legacy has light in it, and also a darkness the church must admit.

share.v: But when Jesus saw it, he was moved with indignation and said to them, “Allow the little children to come to me! Don’t forbid them, for God’s Kingdom belongs to such as these.

blocks.h: In 1 BC an Egyptian worker named Hilarion wrote from Alexandria to his pregnant wife. He wrote in a homely way, and then gave this instruction: if it is a boy, keep it; if it is a girl, throw it out.
This papyrus letter survives today. What makes you stop is its tone. The writer is not brutal. He is simply giving instructions about something many families of the time might have faced.

They were bringing to him little children, that he should touch them, but the disciples rebuked those who were bringing them. But when Jesus saw it, he was moved with indignation and said to them, “Allow the little children to come to me! Don’t forbid them, for God’s Kingdom belongs to such as these.
A beginning decided by the father

In the Greco-Roman world, whether a newborn was kept was often decided by the head of the household. In the Politics Aristotle argued that deformed children should not be raised. In On Anger Seneca discusses the drowning of weak or abnormal newborns as an example of reason. Some of the abandoned children died, and some were picked up, raised and made slaves or prostitutes.

Today we register a baby’s birth because once he is born, he is a person. In many ancient places the “registration” counted only when the head of the household nodded. A child’s worth was like an application form that had not yet been stamped.
A small group said: we do not throw children away

In the middle of the second century the martyr Justin, in chapter 27 of his First Apology, writes that Christians have been taught that it is wicked to abandon newborns, because abandoned children are almost all raised for prostitution. An earlier teaching manual, the Didache (Teaching of the Twelve Apostles), flatly forbids killing newborn babies.

To be fair, this was not a Christian monopoly. Jewish writers such as Philo and Josephus had long condemned abandoning infants, and the church took over this Jewish legacy. In AD 374 Valentinian I made infanticide illegal. A law being passed does not mean the practice disappears, and abandonment of infants did not die out in Christian societies either.
From Bristol to Dohnavur

items: George Müller (1805–1898): from 1849 he built orphan houses on Ashley Down in Bristol and cared for 10,024 orphans over his lifetime. He drew no salary and never asked anyone for funds. There were also critics at the time who said his education lifted poor children “above their station.”
Robert Raikes: in 1780 in Gloucester he hired four women to teach poor children on Sundays. By 1787 the Sunday school movement had reached about 250,000 pupils.
Thomas Barnardo (1845–1905): in 1870 he opened his first boys’ home in London, and from 1871 he announced that no destitute child would be turned away.

Amy Carmichael: she went to India in 1895. In 1901 she took in Preena, a seven-year-old girl who had escaped, and the same year founded the Dohnavur Fellowship, which later sheltered more than a thousand children.
Swanson and Compassion International: it began in 1952 because of Korean War orphans, and in 2023 it had helped more than 2 million people.

blocks.h: As for research, a six-country study published in the Journal of Political Economy in 2013 found that children who had received international sponsorship had clearly better outcomes as adults in years of schooling, completion of schooling and employment.
The other side of the same history

Barnardo produced exaggerated “before and after” photographs for fundraising. From 1882 his organization sent children to Canada, and by 1905 more than 11,000 had gone. Many were wrongly told they were orphans, and on arrival they suffered forced labor and abuse.

The orphanage model itself has also been reexamined. A 2020 systematic review in The Lancet Psychiatry found that institutional care is associated with poorer physical growth and poorer cognitive and attention development, with marked recovery after children leave institutions for families. A randomized study from the Bucharest Early Intervention Project also found that young children placed in foster families had better cognition, and that the earlier the placement, the greater the gain. Today’s consensus leans toward giving priority to supporting birth families, kinship care, adoption and stable foster care.

In the nineteenth century Müller’s orphanage was a lifeboat. In an age with no welfare system it saved countless lives. The lifeboat’s achievement is real, but today there is no need to keep children living on the lifeboat, because we now know how to bring them ashore.
Let us separate the claims and mark how certain each one is.
Child abandonment was widespread in the Greco-Roman world, and classical authors (Aristotle, Seneca) discuss it explicitly. Early Christian writings (the Didache, Justin) clearly oppose it.
The ministries and main dates of Müller, Barnardo, Raikes and Carmichael can be traced in historical sources; the numbers come from institutional or biographical records.

There has indeed been large-scale child sexual abuse and cover-up in the church: in the American Catholic Church from 1950 to 2002, 4,392 clergy faced credible accusations involving 10,667 minors; a French independent commission in 2021 estimated about 216,000 children abused by clergy and members of religious orders since 1950; and a 2022 investigation commissioned by the Southern Baptist Convention also exposed long-standing concealment. These figures come from separate investigations using different methods and cannot be compared directly with one another.

The rise of Christianity was one important force in the decline of the culture of infant abandonment. Scholars broadly agree that the early Christians took a clear stand, but how much influence this had on law and social change is still debated.

Institutional care has a clear negative association with child development, and family-based care does better; the quality of individual institutions and the circumstances of the children vary greatly.

Every child has an inalienable dignity because they are made by God and loved by Christ. This is an inference of faith that history itself cannot prove; many non-Christians also uphold and practice children’s rights.
A dialogue of viewpoints
How much did Christianity actually change?

items.h: Christians brought the Jewish ethic of life into the Gentile world, and together with Jesus’ own example of welcoming children, this slowly made “the child is a person” a presupposition of civilization. This thread has documentary support.

Stoic thought, demographic and economic change and imperial law also played a part. In Song-dynasty China there were foundling homes, and the charitable halls of various religions also cared for abandoned children. The church itself also harmed children in its institutions, so the credit cannot all be given to faith.

blocks.h: He is the father of the fatherless
The God of the Bible stands again and again on the side of those with the least voice. In a world where a father could decide a child’s life or death, this sentence carries great weight.
A father of the fatherless, and a defender of the widows, is God in his holy habitation.
Some of the harshest words Jesus ever spoke were for those who harm the little ones. This sentence does not allow the church to excuse itself with “don’t air the family’s dirty laundry.”

Whoever receives one such little child in my name receives me, but whoever causes one of these little ones who believe in me to stumble, it would be better for him if a huge millstone were hung around his neck and that he were sunk in the depths of the sea.

If you or someone near you has been harmed in the church or at home: it is not your fault. God does not want you to stay silent for the sake of the church’s reputation, and He does not require you to forgive first in order to be spiritual. Please go first to a safe place, find someone you trust, and seek help from the police, a child protection agency or a professional counselor; in Taiwan you can call the 113 protection hotline. If the church asks you to “handle it privately,” you still have the right to make a report.

The center of the gospel is that this Father paid the price Himself. For all the children abandoned in human history, Christ on the cross also cried out the pain of being forsaken. He does not make excuses for the harm. He bore sin and rose from the dead, so that all who are lonely may have a home to come to.
But when the fullness of the time came, God sent out his Son, born to a woman, born under the law, that he might redeem those who were under the law, that we might receive the adoption as children.
I will not leave you orphans. I will come to you.
Take out a photo of yourself as a child, or think of a child you know. Look at that face, be quiet for a minute, and say the child’s name to God.
Meditate: is my attitude toward children more like the disciples who rebuked them, or like Jesus, who was indignant and took the children into His arms?

Prayer: Father in heaven, You are the father of the fatherless. Comfort those who were hurt in childhood and never heard. Make the church the safest place for children. If we have been silent or covered things up, forgive us and give us the courage to tell the truth. Thank You, Lord Jesus, for dying and rising for us, so that we can call You Abba, Father. In the name of Jesus, amen.
321 Life Application

items: Jesus is my example: He stopped His journey to hold children. Today, when you speak with a child, crouch down first, put the phone away, and listen to the end of what he says.

People matter more than tasks: the church’s reputation and the smooth running of meetings can never rank above a child’s safety. Ministry to children needs two adults present, background checks and a reporting system.
Letting God be God and people be people: pastors and spiritual parents are human, and must be held accountable. Spiritual authority is never a license to harm people or to require their silence.

blocks.h: This week: ask your church or fellowship whether it has a written child protection policy. If not, invite your coworkers to draw one up together. You could also begin regular sponsorship of a child, or look after a foster or single-parent family.
Pass it on: how do you think a society learned to treat children as “persons”?
Quiz

quiz.q: In his First Apology, what reasons does Justin give against abandoning newborns?
o: Abandoned children were almost all raised for prostitution
Roman law prescribed severe punishment for abandonment
Abandonment would bring famine
quiz.e: He pointed to the wretched fate of abandoned children and said Christians had been taught that this is wicked.

quiz.q: What is the main conclusion of modern research on institutional orphanages?
o: Institutional care and family care are exactly the same
Children in institutional care can never recover
Institutional care is associated with poorer development, with marked recovery after moving into a family
quiz.e: Research supports giving priority to supporting families, kinship care, adoption and stable foster care; many children recover markedly after leaving institutions.

quiz.q: If someone is abused in a church, which of the following best fits this unit’s reminder?
o: Keep silent first for the sake of the church’s reputation
First go to a safe place and seek a trusted person, the police or professional help
You must forgive the other person before you may ask for help
quiz.e: Safety comes first. Forgiveness is another long road. It is not a precondition for seeking help, and it cannot replace making a report.

units.title: Writing and Literacy
units.sub: Some were put to death so that plowboys could read the Bible; others built alphabets for peoples who had no writing. Wherever the gospel goes, it often begins with a dictionary.

share.v: Your word is a lamp to my feet, and a light for my path.

blocks.h: Taiwan’s first printed newspaper came out in Tainan in 1885, and it was not printed in Chinese characters.

It was called the Tâi-oân-hú-siânn Kàu-hoē-pò (Taiwan Prefectural City Church News), and it spelled Taiwanese in Roman letters. The missionary Thomas Barclay wanted grandmothers, farmers and anyone who had never attended a village school to be able to read God’s word for themselves. A hundred and forty years later, the paper is still in print.
Your word is a lamp to my feet, and a light for my path.
A whole alphabet for the sake of one book

In the fourth century, Bishop Ulfilas (about 311–383) preached to the Goths. Tradition says he created the Gothic alphabet for them and translated the earliest Bible in a Germanic language. In the ninth century the brothers Constantine (Cyril) and Methodius went to Moravia, designed the Glagolitic alphabet for the Slavs and translated Scripture for them. Their disciples later developed the Cyrillic alphabet in Bulgaria, still used today for Russian, Bulgarian and other languages.

Imagine you want to write to a friend and discover that his language has no writing at all. Most people would tell him to learn yours first. These missionaries chose to build a skeleton for his mother tongue.
Putting the Bible in the hands of the plowman

Luther translated the New Testament into German in 1522 and finished the whole Bible in 1534, visiting nearby towns to hear how ordinary people actually spoke. William Tyndale (about 1494–1536) translated the English New Testament from Greek and had it printed in Worms in 1526; he was later executed as a heretic. Foxe records that he once told a clergyman he would make a plowboy know more of Scripture than he did. The fiercest opponents of these translators often came from the church itself.
Morrison and the Union Version

Robert Morrison reached China in 1807 and completed his New Testament in 1813. The whole Bible, done with William Milne, was printed from wooden blocks in 21 volumes in 1823. His Dictionary of the Chinese Language was printed in Macau from 1815 to 1823, running to 4,595 pages, the first two-way Chinese-English dictionary. He spent 27 years in China, and only 10 people were baptized.

In 1919 the Chinese Union Version (官話和合本) appeared. As early as 1920, Zhou Zuoren predicted that translations like it would be closely tied to the future of China’s new literature, and scholars also believe it had considerable influence on the vernacular writing of the May Fourth era. It was not the only source of the vernacular movement; Ming and Qing vernacular novels already existed.

Missionaries were not the only drivers of writing. King Sejong’s creation of Hunminjeongeum, Buddhists copying and printing sutras, and the copying and transmission of the Qur’an in the Islamic world all advanced literacy greatly.
Pe̍h-ōe-jī and Taiwan

Pe̍h-ōe-jī (白話字) was brought to Taiwan by Presbyterian missionaries, and Barclay’s church newspaper made it widespread. In 1942 the Japanese government banned the paper; in 1955 the Nationalist government forbade evangelizing in Pe̍h-ōe-jī, and after the paper was banned again in 1969 it switched to Chinese characters. Restrictions loosened only slowly after martial law ended in 1987.
Literacy and democracy: a debate not yet settled

In 2009 Becker and Woessmann, using nineteenth-century Prussian data, argued that Protestant regions were wealthier mainly because Bible reading drove literacy, rather than because of the work ethic Weber described. In 2012 Woodberry argued in the American Political Science Review that the historical presence of conversionary Protestant missionaries explains about half of the variation in democracy across Africa, Asia and elsewhere. In 2021 Nikolova and Polansky redid the analysis with 26 democracy indicators and found that the association does not hold up.
Let’s look at each claim separately and mark how certain it is.
The Tâi-oân-hú-siânn Kàu-hoē-pò, founded by Barclay in 1885 and printed in Pe̍h-ōe-jī, was Taiwan’s first printed newspaper; Pe̍h-ōe-jī was restricted under both Japanese rule and martial law.
The dates of Morrison’s Chinese Bible and dictionary, Tyndale’s English New Testament of 1526, and Luther’s German Bibles of 1522 and 1534 are all well documented.
The Cyrillic alphabet descends from the disciples of Cyril and Methodius; Ulfilas’s creation of the Gothic alphabet is the traditional account, and his life cannot be fully reconstructed.

As of August 2025, of the world’s 7,396 languages, 544 (about 36.8 million people) are still waiting for translation to begin, and 4,457 are in progress. These are the translation agencies’ own statistics, and meeting the standard does not mean readers can truly read it.

The long-term influence of missions on democracy and education is still disputed: Woodberry’s argument is strong, but replication studies push back. The link between Protestantism and literacy is firmer in the Prussian data, though whether it generalizes is still debated.
God cares that people can read His word for themselves, which is why translation and education have roots in the faith. This is an interpretation of faith, and history alone cannot prove it.
Perspectives Room
Are missions and local languages a blessing or a harm?

items.h: Translating the Bible into a mother tongue declares that this language deserves to carry God’s word. Many languages received their first written record this way and were preserved.

Outsiders decided the alphabet, and it was often tied to colonial education; in some places mission schools suppressed local languages. Canada’s residential schools are a painful example. Whether translation brings dignity depends on whether local people lead.

blocks.h: God speaks words people can understand
After the return from exile, Ezra led the people in reading the Law. The Levites did not only read it aloud but explained it, because understanding is what counts.
They read in the book, in the law of God, distinctly; and they gave the sense, so that they understood the reading.
On the day of Pentecost, the first sign of the Holy Spirit’s coming was that everyone heard their own mother tongue. God did not require everyone to learn a sacred language first.

When this sound was heard, the multitude came together and were bewildered, because everyone heard them speaking in his own language. They were all amazed and marveled, saying to one another, “Behold, aren’t all these who speak Galileans? How do we hear, everyone in our own native language?

The deepest translation took place in Bethlehem. God’s Word became a person and, through a human language, human tears and human scars, let us know Him. On the cross He bought with His blood people from every language.
The Word became flesh and lived among us. We saw his glory, such glory as of the only born Son of the Father, full of grace and truth.
They sang a new song, saying, “You are worthy to take the book and to open its seals, for you were killed, and bought us for God with your blood out of every tribe, language, people, and nation,
Open your Bible and slowly read Psalm 119:105 three times, in the language you know best. If you speak a mother tongue or dialect, read it once more in that, and notice what feels different inside.
Reflect: Many people paid with their lives so that I could pick up this book. When was the last time I gladly opened it?

Pray: God who speaks, You came to find me in words I can understand. Thank You for sending the Lord Jesus, the Word made flesh, who died and rose again for me. Thank You for the translators and copyists I will never know. Let Your word be a lamp to my feet, and help me pass this light to those who are still waiting. In Jesus’ name, amen.
321 Life Application

items: The Bible is my standard: Others paid a price so I could read it, so I will read it myself every day instead of relying on retellings, and examine it as the Bereans did.
Change your mindset, change your life, change your lifestyle: Reading Scripture is not collecting information. Let one verse change one decision today.
People matter more than tasks: Elders who cannot read, or find reading hard, are just as loved by God. Literacy is not salvation, and sitting with them to listen or read together is service.

blocks.h: This week: Read a passage of John with an elder, a child or a new friend. Read slowly, listen to their questions, and try reading in their mother tongue.
Pass it on: What was the first book that made you feel it was “speaking to me”?
Quiz

quiz.q: What script did the Taiwan Prefectural City Church News use when it began?
o: Japanese kana
Pe̍h-ōe-jī (Taiwanese spelled in Roman letters)
Classical Chinese characters
quiz.e: Barclay used Pe̍h-ōe-jī so that people who had never attended a village school could read.

quiz.q: What is the current state of Woodberry’s argument about missions and democracy?
o: It has been proved completely correct
No one has ever studied it
It is still disputed, and a 2021 replication pushed back
quiz.e: Woodberry’s statistics are strong, but Nikolova and Polansky, using other indicators, found that the association does not hold.

quiz.q: In Nehemiah 8:8, what did the Levites do besides read the Law?
o: They gave the sense so the people understood
They forbade the people to read
They hid the book
quiz.e: God’s word is meant to be understood, and this is the root of translation and teaching.

units.title: Shangdi in the Ancient Chinese Books
units.sub: The name really is in the old books. Who it refers to, missionaries argued for two hundred years, and even today it cannot be settled in one sentence.

share.v: Yet he didn’t leave himself without witness, in that he did good and gave you rains from the sky and fruitful seasons, filling our hearts with food and gladness.

blocks.h: In April 1873 a Scottish missionary in his fifties arrived in Beijing and climbed to the Temple of Heaven. There he took off his shoes. His name was James Legge, the man who translated the Four Books and Five Classics into English and who three years later became Oxford’s first professor of Chinese. Why would a minister feel he was standing on holy ground at the very place where China’s emperors offered sacrifice to Heaven?
Because he had read lines like this: “Vast is Shangdi, ruler of the people below” (蕩蕩上帝，下民之辟). That line was written several hundred years before Paul.
Yet he didn’t leave himself without witness, in that he did good and gave you rains from the sky and fruitful seasons, filling our hearts with food and gladness.
The original words in the ancient books
You can check the following four passages yourself by opening the books:

items: Book of Songs, Greater Odes, “Dang”: “Vast is Shangdi, ruler of the people below. Fierce is Shangdi, and his decrees are many and unjust. Heaven gave birth to the multitudes, but his decrees are not to be trusted. All have a beginning, but few see it through to the end.” (蕩蕩上帝，下民之辟。疾威上帝，其命多辟。天生烝民，其命匪諶。靡不有初，鮮克有終。)
Book of Songs, Greater Odes, “Daming”: “This King Wen was careful and reverent; he served Shangdi with brightness and brought many blessings.” (維此文王，小心翼翼。昭事上帝，聿懷多福。)
Book of Songs, Greater Odes, “Huangyi”: “Majestic is Shangdi, gazing down in radiance. He surveys the four quarters, seeking the settled good of the people.” (皇矣上帝，臨下有赫。監觀四方，求民之莫。)
Book of Documents, “Oath of Tang”: “The house of Xia is guilty. I fear Shangdi, and dare not fail to set it right.” (夏氏有罪。予畏上帝，不敢不正。)

blocks.h: These lines portray a ruler who is above, who watches, who can be angry, and who cares for the people. Reading this, it is natural for a Christian’s heart to warm. But not so fast. Read on.

It is like finding a yellowed photograph in Grandma’s old album, and the eyes and brow of the man in it look exactly like someone in your family. The resemblance is real, but whether he is your great-grandfather you still have to check in the household registry. Some people see it and cry, “That’s him!” Others say, “Plenty of people look alike.” The Shangdi of the ancient books is that photograph.
“Di” on the oracle bones

An earlier form of the term appears in the oracle-bone divinations of the Shang dynasty. Di governed weather, harvests and success in war, could issue commands, and could also send disaster. The Shang approached Di through their ancestors, and there are no records of sacrifices offered to Di the way they were offered to other spirits. After the Zhou replaced the Shang, Shangdi and “Heaven” (天) gradually merged; the two are interchangeable in Western Zhou bronze inscriptions, and the Han scholar Zheng Xuan simply explained Shangdi as another name for Heaven.

Scholars do not agree. In 1990 Robert Eno questioned the consensus that the Shang had a single supreme god, arguing that Di in the divinations may be a collective term for a group of spirits, a generic term for some unnamed spirit, or an honorific for a Shang king’s father. Other scholars disagree with this view, and the discussion is not finished.
The translation dispute: two hundred years over one word

items: Catholics: Matteo Ricci used “Shangdi” at times; in 1715 Pope Clement XI issued Ex illa die, fixing “Tianzhu” (天主) as the term and forbidding the Chinese rites. In 1721 the Kangxi Emperor banned Christian teaching.

Protestants: Morrison used “Shen” (神). In the nineteenth century Walter Medhurst argued for “Shangdi,” while William Boone insisted on “Shen,” and British and American missionaries debated it fiercely.

Legge: At first he followed Morrison in using “Shen,” but in the 1850s, influenced by Chinese colleagues such as He Jinshan and Hong Rengan, he came to see “Shangdi” as the right translation and defended it in a book in 1852.
The outcome: There is none. The Chinese Union Version is still printed in both a “Shen” edition and a “Shangdi” edition, and the one in your hands is a relic of this dispute.

blocks.h: The sources for these historical facts are given in the Verify step.
Is the ancient Shangdi the God of the Bible?

items.h: Legge believed the Chinese had kept a surviving knowledge of the true God, and the Singapore Chinese author Chan Kei Thong, in Faith of Our Fathers, goes further and argues that the two are “the same One,” so that for Chinese people the gospel is a return to the faith of their ancestors. The strength of this view is that it tears down the wall of “foreign religion.”

God has revealed Himself to all peoples (Romans 1, Acts 14), and the ancients’ knowledge of Shangdi was a real response, but partial and mixed. The similarities can serve as a bridge without asserting that the identity is the same.

Boone’s camp worried that Shangdi was the name of a god within a pagan system, later confused with the Daoist Jade Emperor; God’s name should not be borrowed from another form of worship. Some Christians today use only “Shen” for the same reason.
